title: Europe’s defence-AI champion Helsing is using Rakuten to break into Japan’s arms market
excerpt: Japan’s army is field-testing Helsing’s HX-2 strike drone, with Rakuten smoothing the German AI defence startup’s path into a market that has only just opened to foreign weapons.
content_html:
Helsing, the Munich startup that has become Europe’s best-funded defence-AI company, is pushing into Asia, and it has found an unlikely guide.

The German firm has enlisted Japan’s Rakuten, a name better known for e-commerce and mobile phones, to help broker the sale of its unmanned systems to Japan’s Ground Self-Defence Forces.

At the centre of the effort is the HX-2, a compact AI-guided strike drone that Japan’s military is putting through field trials due to run until the end of September.

Alongside the drone, Helsing sells AI software for battlefield analysis, underwater surveillance and combat aircraft, the software-first arsenal that has made it one of Europe’s most valuable tech firms and a poster child for the continent’s rearmament.

The conglomerate is positioning itself as a broker that can walk foreign defence startups through Japan’s notoriously opaque procurement system, and it has done this before, having helped the Ukrainian drone-software firm Swarmer show its tech to Japanese units.

In a market where the paperwork can be as formidable as the competition, a trusted local name is worth a great deal.

The timing is deliberate. Japan is in the middle of its biggest military build-up in decades, driven by an increasingly assertive China and a war in Ukraine that has rewritten every assumption about drones, and it eased its long-standing arms-export and procurement rules earlier this year.

That has thrown open a market foreign weapons-makers could barely touch before, and Helsing is far from the only one now circling it.

Tokyo has committed to lifting defence spending toward levels not seen in the postwar era, and every yen of that budget is a magnet for exactly the kind of autonomous, software-led kit the war in Ukraine has made fashionable.

A company built on online shopping and mobile networks recasting itself as a matchmaker for weapons startups is a measure of how far the defence boom has spread beyond the traditional primes, pulling in financiers, cloud providers and consumer-tech names chasing a market suddenly awash with government money.

Across Europe and Asia alike, capital and engineers are pouring into anything that promises an edge on a modern battlefield.

Founded only in 2021, it raised billions this year, ranks among Europe’s most valuable private tech firms, and has become a primary supplier of drones to Ukraine with Berlin’s backing.

Its pitch, that modern warfare is increasingly won by software and autonomy rather than sheer hardware, has made it the continent’s clearest bet that AI belongs at the heart of defence.

That reputation is not spotless, though. Earlier this year Ukraine paused further orders of the HX-2 after technical problems in the field, a reminder that the distance between an impressive AI demo and a reliable battlefield weapon can be wide. Japan’s own trials, with another month left to run, will be watched closely for exactly that reason.

The Japan move also fits a company expanding on every front. Helsing has been building an AI submarine, striking an alliance with Mistral on military AI, and casting itself as a pillar of Europe’s scramble to rearm.

Selling into Asia extends that ambition well beyond NATO, and quietly turns a European champion into a would-be global arms supplier.

Whether the Rakuten partnership converts trials into contracts is still unknown, and Japan remains a cautious buyer with a long procurement memory.

But the very fact that a European AI startup barely five years old is testing strike drones for the Japanese army, with an e-commerce giant as its fixer, captures how fast the business of war is being remade, and how eagerly its new players are rushing in.

content_html_zh:
慕尼黑初创公司赫尔辛 (Helsing) 已成为欧洲资金最雄厚的国防人工智能公司，正在进军亚洲，并且找到了一个意想不到的指导。

这家德国公司已聘请日本乐天（一家以电子商务和移动电话而闻名的公司）帮助其向日本陆上自卫队出售其无人系统。

这项工作的核心是 HX-2，这是一种紧凑型人工智能制导攻击无人机，日本军方正在进行现场试验，预计运行到 9 月底。

除了无人机之外，赫尔辛还销售用于战场分析、水下监视和战斗机的人工智能软件，这种以软件为先的武器库使其成为欧洲最有价值的科技公司之一，也是欧洲大陆重新武装的典范。

该集团将自己定位为一个经纪人，可以引导外国国防初创公司通过日本臭名昭著的不透明采购系统，而且它以前也这样做过，帮助乌克兰无人机软件公司 Swarmer 向日本单位展示其技术。

在一个文书工作与竞争一样激烈的市场中，一个值得信赖的本地品牌非常有价值。

时机是经过深思熟虑的。 日本正处于数十年来最大规模的军事集结之中，其推动因素是日益自信的中国和乌克兰战争，这场战争改写了有关无人机的所有假设，并且今年早些时候放宽了长期存在的武器出口和采购规则。

这打开了一个外国武器制造商以前几乎无法触及的市场，而赫尔辛远不是现在唯一一个围绕这个市场的市场。

东京已承诺将国防开支提高到战后时代未曾见过的水平，而预算中的每一日元都吸引着乌克兰战争所流行的那种以软件为主导的自主装备。

一家建立在在线购物和移动网络基础上的公司将自己重塑为武器初创公司的牵线搭桥，这可以衡量国防热潮已经超出了传统的主导地位，吸引了金融家、云提供商和消费科技公司追逐突然充斥着政府资金的市场。

在欧洲和亚洲，资本和工程师正在涌入任何能够在现代战场上占据优势的领域。

该公司成立于 2021 年，今年筹集了数十亿美元，跻身欧洲最有价值的私营科技公司之列，并在柏林的支持下成为乌克兰无人机的主要供应商。

它的主张是，现代战争越来越多地通过软件和自主性而不是纯粹的硬件来赢得胜利，这使其成为非洲大陆最明确的赌注，即人工智能属于国防的核心。

不过，这种声誉并非一尘不染。 今年早些时候，由于现场出现技术问题，乌克兰暂停了 HX-2 的进一步订购，这提醒人们，令人印象深刻的人工智能演示与可靠的战场武器之间的距离可能很大。 正是出于这个原因，日本自己的审判还剩下一个月，将受到密切关注。

进军日本也适合一家在各方面扩张的公司。 赫尔辛一直在建造一艘人工智能潜艇，与米斯特拉尔在军事人工智能方面结成联盟，并将自己打造成欧洲重新武装的中流砥柱。

向亚洲销售的野心远远超出了北约的范围，并悄悄地将欧洲冠军变成了潜在的全球武器供应商。

乐天合作是否会将试验转化为合同仍不得而知，日本仍然是一个谨慎的买家，有着悠久的采购记忆。

但事实是，一家成立仅五年的欧洲人工智能初创公司正在为日本军队测试攻击无人机，并由一家电子商务巨头作为其解决者，这一事实体现了战争业务正在以多么快的速度重塑，以及新参与者涌入的热情。
